opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the biggest one is really the question of how well our task distribution maps onto the real-world work people actually care about. The headline number, that the length of tasks models can complete with 50% reliability has been doubling roughly every seven months, is measured on a particular suite of tasks: software engineering, ML engineering, some cybersecurity, some general reasoning. They're tasks we can score automatically and that run in a sandboxed environment. That's what makes the measurement possible at all, but it's also what makes it potentially unrepresentative.

Real tasks tend to be "messier." They have underspecified goals, you need to gather context from colleagues or a big codebase you didn't write, there's no clean scoring function, feedback is delayed, and you often have to coordinate with other people or recover from things going wrong in ways nobody anticipated. We did try to look at this. We rated tasks on a messiness score, and models do perform worse on the messier ones, but the trend over time looks fairly similar. So the slope seems reasonably robust, but the absolute level, what "a one-hour task" actually means for a model in a real job, is much more uncertain. You could plausibly be off by a substantial factor in either direction when you translate to real-world usefulness.

Related to that, the human baselines matter a lot. The time horizon is defined by how long it takes a skilled human to do the task, and that depends heavily on who the human is and how much context they have. Our baseliners were competent professionals, but they were new to the specific codebases. Someone who's been working in a repo for years might do the same task many times faster. So the "hours" are in some sense low-context-human hours, and that's a meaningful caveat.

Then there's the reliability threshold. We usually report 50% success because it's statistically the most stable point, but for a lot of practical deployment you need 80, 90, 99% reliability, and the horizon at those thresholds is much shorter, several times shorter. The gap between "can sometimes do it" and "can be trusted to do it" is a big deal for economic impact.

And finally, there's extrapolation uncertainty. Fitting an exponential to a few years of data and projecting forward is useful as a baseline forecast, but whether the trend speeds up, because AI starts accelerating AI research, or slows down, because we hit limits on compute or data or because the remaining skills are qualitatively harder, is genuinely open. Our measurement also gets noisier at the top end, since we have fewer very long tasks, so the most recent and most decision-relevant data points tend to have the widest error bars.

So my summary would be: I'm fairly confident about the direction and rough rate of the trend. I'm much less confident about how to map a given number onto "this model can do X fraction of real jobs." That translation is where most of the uncertainty lives, and it's what we're most actively trying to improve.

r001.rationale: It identifies how well METR’s task distribution maps to real-world work as the biggest uncertainty.

r002.rationale: It discusses the trend and task messiness, but does not express confidence in long horizons on distributions that are easy to improve through iterative feedback.

r003.rationale: It says the mapping from measured horizons to real-world usefulness is highly uncertain.

r004.rationale: It notes that real tasks may lack clean scoring and have delayed feedback, but does not specifically question generalization to tasks whose results are expensive to check.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the biggest one is just how representative our task suite is of real-world work. The headline number people see is something like "models can now do tasks that take humans X hours," and that's measured on a specific set of tasks: software engineering, some ML research, some reasoning stuff, all of them fairly self-contained, clearly specified, with an automatic way to check whether you succeeded. That's a really particular slice of what humans actually do. Real jobs involve ambiguity, figuring out what the task even is, dealing with messy context, interacting with other people, and we don't have good ways to measure any of that. So when we say "50% success at tasks that take humans a few hours," the honest caveat is that this is a few hours of a certain kind of work.

The second thing is the human baseline itself. When we say a task "takes a human two hours," that's based on contractors we hired who were reasonably skilled but didn't have deep context on the codebase or the problem. An expert who already knows the system might do the same thing in twenty minutes. So the time horizon is always relative to some reference population, and shifting that reference changes the number quite a lot. We try to be explicit about it, but it gets lost when the chart gets passed around.

And then the third thing, which I think people underweight, is what the success rate threshold means. We report the length of task where the model succeeds about half the time. But for a lot of real deployment, you care about reliability at 80 or 95 percent, and the horizon at those thresholds is dramatically shorter, like, by a factor of five or more. So "the model can do a two-hour task" and "you can hand the model a two-hour task and walk away" are very different claims, and the headline number supports the first, not the second.

I'd say the trend is more robust than any single point estimate. The doubling time has been pretty consistent across different task subsets and different ways of slicing it, which gives me some confidence that it's measuring something real about capability growth. But if you ask me what the absolute number means for, say, whether a model can autonomously do a week of real research, I'd say we genuinely don't know, and anyone claiming precision there is overclaiming.

astra-6.text:
I think the main uncertainty is how much these estimates tell us about performance on real-world work. The time horizon is the length of task, measured by how long it takes a human, that a model can complete at a particular success rate. It doesn’t mean the model can reliably do any task that takes that long, or that it can work autonomously for that amount of time.

Tasks with the same human completion time can be very different for an AI. And a well-specified task with a clear way to check success is different from a messy project where you have to figure out what the goal is, gather context, and interact with people. So the key question is how representative the tasks we measure are of the work we actually care about. The estimates are useful evidence about capabilities, but translating them into claims about autonomous work requires additional assumptions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main uncertainty is how representative these tasks are of the things we actually care about. The time horizon is the length of task, measured by how long it takes a human, that an AI can complete with a given probability of success. It’s not a claim that the AI can do any job that takes that long, or work autonomously for that amount of time.

Our tasks are mostly fairly well-specified software and reasoning tasks, with a reasonably clear way to check success. Real work often involves figuring out what the task is, getting context from other people, and dealing with things you can’t easily verify. So the big question is how well performance on this task distribution predicts performance on those messier, economically relevant tasks. The trend can be informative while that translation remains quite uncertain.
